lines.text: Two people organized a whole warehouse around the same kinds of tables this chapter has been building, in opposite directions.
Neither of them was simply right. Each one wins on a different thing.
The very definition most people use for a data warehouse comes from the first of these two.
His own approach builds one normalized model for the whole enterprise first, and feeds every department's view from that single model afterward.
The second person's approach runs the opposite direction.
Plan one business process, ship a star schema for it, and share dimensions across every process after that, instead of modeling the whole enterprise before shipping anything.
Picture a team with a hard deadline and only one source system to deal with.
Which of these two gets them to something usable first?
The process-first approach. One star schema, shipped.
Modeling the whole enterprise first is the slower path exactly when the deadline is what matters most.
Here is that speed, made concrete.
One star schema can go live while the enterprise-wide model is still being designed. That is the entire point of building process by process.
Now picture a dozen separate source systems that all need to agree on one thing: what a customer actually is.
Which approach handles that kind of agreement better?
The single enterprise model.
Shared dimensions across stars do real work too, but settling one definition once, in one place, is exactly what that model exists for.
That is the cost the single model is actually paying for.
One definition, agreed on once, instead of re-settling it separately inside every star schema that happens to touch a customer.

tolerated.line: One definition, agreed on once, instead of re-settling it separately inside every star schema that happens to touch a customer.

lines.text: Now picture a business rule that keeps changing, unpredictably, over time.
Does either approach clearly handle that better?
Not cleanly. It depends entirely on what kind of change you mean.
A new process slots into the incremental approach without touching what already exists. A changed rule gets fixed once in a single model instead of chased down everywhere.

tolerated.line: A new process slots into the incremental approach without touching what already exists. A changed rule gets fixed once in a single model instead of chased down everywhere.

lines.text: Both of those are genuinely true at the same time, pointed at different kinds of change.
Neither approach simply wins this one.
Put all three comparisons next to each other and a pattern shows up.
Speed favors one. Agreement across sources favors the other. Tolerance to change depends on what's actually changing. The real choice was never a single verdict.
Now, the shift that changed all of this.
Cloud warehouses built on columns made storage far cheaper and processing far faster than it used to be.
That single shift is why teams stopped having to commit upfront.

When transforming data after it lands is cheap and fast, a team can start with the incremental, process-first approach and fold in that single shared model later, instead of betting on one direction from day one.

tolerated.line: That single shift is why teams stopped having to commit upfront.

lines.text: Two directions, opposite ways of organizing the same kind of warehouse.
The real choice runs against speed, agreement, and tolerance to change, not one preference. And cheap, fast transforms after loading narrowed that choice, without making it disappear.
One more scenario before moving on.
A team has to bring in a new source system on a short, repeating cycle, with no enterprise-wide model agreed on yet. Which approach actually fits that?
The process-first, incremental approach.
It was built specifically to add one process at a time, without waiting on a model nobody has agreed to yet.
